Background Cocoa flavanols (CF) can stimulate vasodilation by improved nitric oxide (NO) synthesis and have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory capacities. This study aimed to examine whether acute CF intake can affect exercise-induced changes in antioxidant capacity, oxidative stress, inflammation and NO production, as well as exercise performance and recovery in well-trained cyclists . Methods Twelve well-trained male cyclists (mean ± SD age, VO2max: 30 ± 3 years, 63.0 ± 3.5 ml/kg/min) participated in this randomized, double-blind, cross over study. On 2 separate occasions, subjects performed two 30-min time trials 1.5 (TT1) and 3 (TT2) hours after CF (900 mg CF) or placebo (PL, 13 mg CF) intake, interposed by passive rest. Lactate, glucose, heartrate, rating of perceived exertion (RPE) and power output were measured during the TTs. Blood was drawn at baseline, before and after each TT and analyzed for epicatechin serum concentrations, trolox equivalent antioxidative capacity (TEAC), uric acid (UA), malonaldehyde (MDA), L-arginine/ADMA, citrulline, interleukin (IL)-1, IL-6 and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α plasma concentrations. Relative changes in blood markers and pacing strategy during TT were analysed by repeated measured ANOVA. TT performance was compared between PL and CF by paired t-test. Results Epicatechin concentrations were increased by CF intake. Exercise-induced increase in TEAC/UA was improved by CF intake (F(1) = 5.57; p = .038) (post-TT1: PL: 113.34 ± 3.9%, CF: 117.64 ± 3.96%, post-TT2: PL: 108.59 ± 3.95%, CF: 123.72 ± 7.4% to baseline), while exercise-induced increases in MDA, IL-1 and IL-6 were not affected by CF intake. TNF-α was unaltered by exercise and by CF. Exercise-induced decreases in L-arginine/ADMA and increases in citrulline were not affected by CF intake. TT1 and TT2 performance and exercise-induced physiological changes were unaffected by CF intake. Conclusion Acute CF intake increased total antioxidant capacity in rest and during exercise, but did not affect exercise-induced lipid peroxidation, inflammation, nor NO production in healthy athletes. Acute CF intake did not improve TT performance and recovery. Trial registration ISRCTN32875 , 21-11-2016, retrospectively registered. Keywords Cocoa Flavanols Oxidative stress Nitric oxide Exercise issue-copyright-statement © The Author(s) 2017 Background A balanced and well-chosen nutrient intake is not only crucial for a healthy lifestyle, but also for optimal sport performance. There is a widespread use of dietary antioxidants, including vitamin E, resveratrol, beetroot, quercetin and cocoa flavanols (CF) in the athletic field. The main flavanols in cocoa are epicatechin, catechin (monomers) and procyanidins (oligomers). Their antioxidant (and in some situations perhaps pro-oxidant) effect is determined by the tricyclic structure of the flavanols. In vitro and in vivo studies clearly show that CF have a strong antioxidant capacity [ 1 , 2 ]. However, the potential role of chronic or acute CF intake to counteract exercise-induced oxidative stress and its effect on exercise performance is still unclear [ 3 – 7 ]. Oxidative stress refers to the imbalance between oxidants and antioxidants in favor of the oxidants, leading to a disruption of redox signaling and/or molecular damage [ 8 ]. During exhaustive exercise, NADPH oxidase-derived formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) results in an altered redox state in the muscle [ 9 ]. In contrast to the initial belief that nutritional antioxidant intake would be beneficial for exercise performance by protecting the body against oxidative stress, it is now hypothesized that exercise-induced oxidative stress promotes the expression of antioxidant defence and the adaptive responses to training [ 10 ]. However, when exercise-induced ROS formation exceeds the antioxidant capacity, oxidative stress occurs with detrimental effects on proteins, lipids and DNA, possibly leading to contractile muscle dysfunction, accelerated muscle-fatigue and reduced exercise performance [ 11 ]. Thus, at moments when optimal exercise performance is key and training adaptations are of minor importance (e.g. competition), acute intake of antioxidants may help scavenge free radicals and therefore directly prevent a decline in exercise performance and optimize post-exercise recovery [ 9 , 12 ]. In the recent years, CF have also been discovered as potent anti-inflammatory agents [ 13 ]. Exhaustive exercise can cause inflammation [ 14 ], resulting in a potential role for CF as a nutritional intervention to prevent exercise-induced muscle damage. Nevertheless, Allgrove et al. [ 6 ] did not find any beneficial effect of 2 week CF (108 mg) intake on exercise-induced inflammatory markers. Independent from its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, CF are also known to stimulate vasodilation through increased nitric oxide (NO) availability [ 15 ]. In vitro experiments demonstrated that CF lead to the inhibition of arginase, resulting in a greater L-Arginine availability, the substrate of endothelial NO synthase (eNOS) [ 16 ]. In vitro [ 17 ] and in vivo [ 18 , 19 ] experiments showed that CF intake activates eNOS, which converts L-Arginine, in the presence of molecular oxygen, to NO and citrulline. Besides its role in vasodilation, NO can also react at a diffusion-controlled rate with superoxide to form the highly reactive oxidant peroxynitrite. Consequently, by elevating NO production, CF might hypothetically have a pro-oxidant effect. However, because of its antioxidant capacity, CF can reduce ROS formation (e.g. superoxide) and repress the formation of peroxynitrite, thus elevating NO availability [ 20 ]. Based on the fact that NO modulates blood flow and mitochondrial respiration during exercise [ 21 , 22 ], it has been suggested that increased NO production may enhance oxygen and nutrient delivery to active muscles, as well as improve mitochondrial efficiency, hence improving tolerance to physical exercise and recovery mechanisms [ 21 ]. Although many athletes use supplements of NO because of their potential ergogenic role, the scientific evidence is very scarce [ 21 ]. eNOS activity and thus NO production are stimulated by exercise-induced shear stress and thus strongly depend on training status [ 23 ]. This suggests a minimal effect for CF and other nutritional supplements on eNOS activity and NO production in healthy trained athletes without vascular restrictions. Whether CF supplementation can alter NO production during exercise, and whether it may improve exercise performance and recovery in well-trained athletes, remains elusive [ 5 – 7 ]. Therefore, the aims of this study were to examine the effects of CF intake on: i) indirect markers of eNOS dependent NO synthesis, L-arginine and citrulline, during exhaustive exercise ii) exercise-induced changes in antioxidant capacity, oxidative stress and inflammation, and iii) exercise performance and recovery in well-trained athletes. We hypothesized that CF intake i) will have little effect on indirect markers of NO production and exercise performance in these healthy, well-trained, subjects, but ii) will decrease exercise-induced oxidative stress and inflammation, leading to an improved recovery.

extracted_data.document_summary: This randomized, double-blind, cross-over study investigated the effects of acute cocoa flavanol (CF) intake on exercise-induced changes in antioxidant capacity, oxidative stress, inflammation, nitric oxide (NO) production, exercise performance, and recovery in well-trained male cyclists. Findings showed acute CF intake increased systemic epicatechin levels and total antioxidant capacity (TEAC/UA and UA), but did not significantly affect exercise-induced lipid peroxidation (MDA), inflammation (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α), or NO production markers (L-arginine/ADMA, citrulline). While CF intake showed a tendency for improved late-stage performance in the first time trial, overall exercise performance and recovery were not significantly enhanced.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute cocoa flavanol (CF) intake and cycling exercise
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Participants received an acute dose of either 903.75 mg of cocoa flavanols (CF) or a placebo (15 mg CF) in chocolate milk prior to exercise. The exercise protocol involved two 30-minute time trials (TT1 and TT2) performed at a workload equivalent to 75% of peak power output, separated by a 100-minute passive recovery. No explicit dose-response comparisons were conducted beyond the high-CF vs. placebo design.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased by CF intake (main effect of time: F = 13.23, p < 0.001) before and after TT1 (100-130 min post-intake) and before and after TT2 (230-260 min post-intake). Peak concentration reached approximately 450 nM between 100 and 130 min after intake.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A main monomeric flavanol component of cocoa, a flavonoid metabolite involved in antioxidant defense and potentially vascular function; indicates systemic exposure to cocoa flavanols.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: After acute cocoa flavanol intake prior to exercise (two 30-min time trials) in well-trained cyclists, peaking during the first exercise bout.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Confirms systemic absorption and bioavailability of ingested cocoa flavanols, indicating potential for related physiological effects, though not directly linked to performance enhancement in this study.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Total antioxidant capacity (corrected for uric acid)

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly higher in the CF trial than in the PL trial (main effect of trial: F(1) = 5.57; p = .038). Exercise-induced increases in TEAC/UA were improved by CF intake. Post-TT1: PL: 113.34 ± 3.9%, CF: 117.64 ± 3.96% to baseline; Post-TT2: PL: 108.59 ± 3.95%, CF: 123.72 ± 7.4% to baseline. After each TT, TEAC/UA was significantly increased compared to concentrations before the TT (main effect of time: F(4) = 11.84; p < 0.001). Before TT2, TEAC/UA was significantly lower compared to after TT1.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Assesses total plasma antioxidant defense capacity, controlling for the contribution of uric acid, providing a refined view by accounting for exercise-induced UA changes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During exhaustive exercise (two 30-min time trials) after acute cocoa flavanol intake in well-trained cyclists.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates enhanced total antioxidant capacity, suggesting improved ability to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reduce oxidative stress, specifically the non-uric acid related antioxidant defense.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (due to exercise), unchanged (by CF intake)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Plasma concentrations significantly increased after TT1 compared to before TT1 and before TT2 (main effect of time: F(4) = 2.98; p = 0.029). However, these exercise-induced increases were not affected by acute CF intake.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A reactive aldehyde and an end-product of lipid peroxidation, serving as a biomarker for oxidative damage to lipids and cellular membranes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During exhaustive exercise (primarily after TT1) following acute cocoa flavanol intake in well-trained cyclists.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates acute oxidative stress and cell damage in response to intense exercise; suggests no protective effect of acute CF intake against exercise-induced lipid peroxidation.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (due to exercise), unchanged (by CF intake)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased after TT1 (PL: +12.2 ± 16.0%; CF: +12.8 ± 12.6%) (main effect of time: F(4) = 2.96; p = .03). TT2 did not induce significant increases. Exercise-induced increases were not affected by acute CF intake.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in the initiation and amplification of immune responses and inflammation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: After the first exhaustive time trial (TT1) following acute cocoa flavanol intake in well-trained cyclists.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates an acute inflammatory response triggered by intense exercise (TT1); suggests no anti-inflammatory effect of acute CF intake on this exercise-induced response.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (due to exercise), unchanged (by CF intake)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased after TT1 (PL: +64.9 ± 10.5%; CF: +70.2 ± 14.2%) (main effect of time: F(4) = 18.88; p < 0.001). TT2 did not induce significant increases. Exercise-induced increases were not affected by acute CF intake.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A pleiotropic cytokine with both pro- and anti-inflammatory roles, often elevated during and after exercise, and functions as a myokine to regulate muscle metabolism.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: After the first exhaustive time trial (TT1) following acute cocoa flavanol intake in well-trained cyclists.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates an acute inflammatory response and metabolic signaling to intense exercise (TT1); suggests no anti-inflammatory effect of acute CF intake on this exercise-induced response, which is not considered detrimental for muscle metabolism.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: TNF-α levels were unaltered by both exercise (TTs) and acute CF intake (data not shown/no significant changes reported).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A potent pro-inflammatory cytokine involved in systemic inflammation, immune cell regulation, and apoptosis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During exhaustive exercise (two 30-min time trials) following acute cocoa flavanol intake in well-trained cyclists.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates no significant inflammatory response to the exercise protocol itself and no modulating effect of acute CF intake on this inflammatory marker.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: lower (due to exercise), unchanged (by CF intake)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly decreased in plasma after exercise (both TTs) (main effect of time: F(4) = 3.69; p = .01). Acute CF intake had no effect on the ratio, neither at rest nor in response to exercise-induced decreases.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Regulates nitric oxide (NO) synthesis and bioavailability; L-arginine is a precursor for NO, while Asymmetric Dimethylarginine (ADMA) inhibits NO synthesis. The ratio reflects NO bioavailability and synthesis.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During exhaustive exercise (two 30-min time trials) following acute cocoa flavanol intake in well-trained cyclists.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates modulation of the NO-pathway, which is crucial for vasodilation and blood flow regulation during exercise. Suggests that acute CF intake did not enhance NO production or availability beyond the exercise-induced changes in healthy, well-trained athletes.

analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Plasma concentration (by-product of NO synthesis, Mass Spectrometry)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (due to exercise), unchanged (by CF intake)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased in plasma after exercise (both TTs) (main effect of time: F(4) = 11.88; p < 0.001). Acute CF intake did not affect increases in citrulline, neither at rest nor in response to exercise.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A co-product of nitric oxide (NO) synthesis by endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS); elevated levels typically indicate increased NO production.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During exhaustive exercise (two 30-min time trials) following acute cocoa flavanol intake in well-trained cyclists.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates increased activity of the NO-pathway during exercise; suggests that acute CF intake did not modulate exercise-induced nitric oxide production or eNOS activity.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Did not significantly differ between CF and placebo (PL) intake or between different time points (no main effect of time or trial observed).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A monomeric flavanol component of cocoa, measured to assess systemic exposure to cocoa flavanols.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following consumption of CF-content chocolate milk during exercise trials.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: No significant impact observed in this study context regarding CF intake or exercise on its serum concentration, indicating limited or no absorption/effect compared to epicatechin.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased by acute CF intake compared to placebo (main effect of trial: F(1) = 7.21; p = 0.02). Also significantly increased after TT1 and TT2 compared to pre-TT levels (main effect of time: F(4) = 17.7; p < 0.001). Plasma concentrations were significantly lower before TT2 compared to after TT1.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A major endogenous antioxidant in the blood and a purine metabolism product; contributes significantly to total plasma antioxidant capacity and is upregulated by exercise due to elevated energy-rich purine phosphate catabolism.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: After acute cocoa flavanol intake and during/after exhaustive exercise (two 30-min time trials) in well-trained cyclists.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Contributes to total antioxidant capacity; indicates enhanced antioxidant defense (due to CF intake) and exercise-induced metabolic stress.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: higher (due to exercise), unchanged (by CF intake)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased during both TT1 and TT2 (main effect of time, p < 0.001). Acute CF intake had no effect on blood lactate levels (no main effect of trial or interaction effect).

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: A metabolic byproduct of anaerobic glycolysis, indicating intensity of exercise and energy metabolism.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During exhaustive exercise (two 30-min time trials) following acute cocoa flavanol intake in well-trained cyclists.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects reliance on anaerobic energy production and the intensity of exercise; indicates no impact of CF on exercise metabolism or fatigue markers.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Significantly increased during both TT1 and TT2 (main effect of time, p < 0.001). Acute CF intake had no effect on blood glucose levels (no main effect of trial or interaction effect).
